content: The overall efficacy of the influenza vaccine was 86%, with an efficacy of 87% specifically among children aged 60 to 84 months. The vaccine demonstrated a 92% efficacy in preventing culture-confirmed influenza during a two-season study. Additional findings included a 27% reduction in febrile otitis media and a 28% reduction in otitis media cases requiring concurrent antibiotic use. Administration of the live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) resulted in a 30% lower incidence of febrile otitis media and a 21% reduction in febrile illnesses. A separate study evaluating the effectiveness of LAIV in children aged 18 months to 18 years showed an 18% effectiveness against medically attended acute respiratory illness (MAARI). However, when a validation sample of surveillance cultures was applied, the vaccine demonstrated a 92% efficacy against influenza A (H1N1) and a 66% efficacy against an influenza B drift variant. In healthy adults, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving 4,561 working adults aged 18 to 64 years assessed various outcomes, including reductions in illness, absenteeism, healthcare visits, and medication use during peak and total influenza outbreak periods. This study, conducted during the 1997-1998 influenza season, noted that the vaccine and circulating A (H3N2) strains were not well-matched. No significant difference was observed between LAIV and placebo recipients in terms of febrile episodes during peak outbreak periods. However, vaccination was associated with a 19% reduction in severe febrile illnesses and a 24% reduction in febrile upper respiratory tract illnesses. Vaccinated individuals also experienced fewer days of illness, fewer workdays lost, fewer healthcare visits, and reduced use of prescription antibiotics and over-the-counter medications. Among a subset of 3,637 healthy adults aged 18 to 49 years, LAIV recipients had 26% fewer febrile upper respiratory illness episodes, 27% fewer workdays lost due to febrile upper respiratory illness, and 18% to 37% fewer days with healthcare provider visits caused by febrile illness compared to placebo recipients. Antibiotic use was reduced by 41% to 45% in this age group. Another randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled challenge study involving 92 healthy adults aged 18 to 41 years assessed the efficacy of both LAIV and inactivated influenza vaccine. The overall efficacy of LAIV and the inactivated vaccine in preventing laboratory-documented influenza from all three influenza strains combined was 85% and 71%, respectively. The difference in efficacy between the two vaccines was not statistically significant. Influenza vaccination has been shown to reduce healthcare costs and productivity losses associated with influenza illness. Economic studies in the United States have reported overall societal cost savings and substantial reductions in hospitalization and mortality among individuals aged over 65 years. Among adults aged 65 years and older, vaccination resulted in net savings per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained, with costs ranging from $23 to $256 per QALY among younger age groups. Further studies are needed to evaluate the relative cost-effectiveness and cost utility of influenza vaccination among children and adults under 65 years, accounting for year-to-year variations in influenza attack rates, illness severity, and vaccine efficacy. One of the national health objectives for 2010 was to achieve 90% vaccination coverage among individuals aged over 65 years. Influenza vaccination levels in this group increased from 33% in 1989 to 66% in 1999, surpassing the Healthy People 2000 objective of 60%. The highest recorded vaccine coverage in this group was 68% during the 1999-2000 influenza season. Possible reasons for the increase in vaccination levels include greater acceptance of preventive medical services, increased vaccine delivery by healthcare providers, new information on vaccine effectiveness and safety, and the initiation of Medicare reimbursement for influenza vaccination in 1993. Despite these improvements, vaccination coverage among adults with high-risk conditions aged 18 to 49 years and 50 to 64 years remained substantially lower than the Healthy People 2000 and 2010 objectives of 60%. Continued annual monitoring is necessary to assess the effects of vaccine supply delays, changes in vaccination recommendations, reimbursement rates, and other factors influencing vaccination coverage. New strategies will be required to improve coverage and achieve national health objectives.
